extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners before the USPTO, attorneys facing reciprocal discipline, and USPTO/OED staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for imposing reciprocal discipline on a practitioner under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 based on state disciplinary action, including grounds to defeat reciprocal discipline, burdens of proof, sanctions, and post-discipline administrative requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds to avoid reciprocal discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that: (i) the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process; (ii) there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject; (iii) the imposition of the same ... by the Office would result in a grave injustice; or (iv) any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulatory text mirrors the Selling v. Radford standard. To prevent reciprocal discipline, the respondent must create a genuine issue of material fact as to one of these enumerated criteria by clear and convincing evidence. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent's burden and standard of review
rubrics_metrics.description: In reciprocal-discipline cases the respondent attorney bears the burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal presumption favors imposition of reciprocal discipline based on a state adjudication; the USPTO Director (like a federal court) is not sitting as a court of review to relitigate state findings. See Selling v. Radford, and cases cited (In re Kramer, In re Friedman, In re Zdravkovich, In re Sibley). The standard is narrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of identical sanction absent a successful defense
rubrics_metrics.description: If the practitioner fails to meet the burden, the USPTO Director shall impose the identical sanction ordered by the state (e.g., public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office follows the state-imposed sanction unless a clear-and-convincing showing of one of the § 11.24(d)(1) grounds is made. Prior USPTO decisions apply identical discipline when state sanction falls within appropriate range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice analysis — proportionality and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a respondent contends that imposition of the same discipline would result in grave injustice, the inquiry focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct and allows consideration of mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the state sanction is within the range of appropriate penalties, it generally is not a grave injustice for the USPTO to impose reciprocal discipline. Authorities: In re Thav; In re Kramer; In re Attorney Discipline Matter; In re Benjamin; Persaud v. Director of the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting proof of satisfaction of state-ordered terms (e.g., restitution or training)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the state discipline includes specific terms (such as restitution or required training), the USPTO may require the same term but permit the practitioner to satisfy that term by providing proof that the state-ordered requirement has already been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid duplication or confusion, the Office will accept evidence that a state-ordered term was satisfied (examples: proof of class taken or proof of restitution paid). Relevant USPTO precedents include In re: Arno T. Naeckel and In re Dhand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of misconduct warranting discipline (types of unethical conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct found to warrant suspension included: failing to file design and utility patent applications or otherwise perform work for a client after hire; failing to refund unearned legal fees; depositing client funds for filing costs into a business account and using those funds for personal or business purposes without client authority; engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (knowingly converting client funds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factual examples were violations of Illinois Rules of Professional Conduct: 1.3 (diligence), 1.16(d) (refund unearned fees), 1.15(a) (safeguard client property), and 8.4 (dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation). Such conduct supports reciprocal discipline under 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural timelines for notices, responses, and judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director serves a Request for Notice and Order and the USPTO gives the respondent a set period (e.g., 40 days in this matter) to file a response asserting any grounds under § 11.24(d). Judicial review of the USPTO Director's final decision may be had by petition to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 'within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent's Notice and Order must contain all information they believe sufficient to establish a genuine issue of material fact by clear and convincing evidence. Local E.D. Va. rules (e.g., E.D. Va. Local Civil Rule 83.5) may apply to petitions for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional and regulatory basis for USPTO discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director has jurisdiction under 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19 and 11.24 to impose reciprocal discipline based on state bar adjudications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary proceedings proceed pursuant to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. § 11.101 et seq.) and related OED procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-discipline administrative actions and practitioner obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Following imposition of discipline the Order may require: publication of a Notice of Suspension in the Official Gazette; notice to state disciplinary agencies and courts per 37 C.F.R. § 11.59; compliance with duties enumerated in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; dissociation of the practitioner's name from any USPTO Customer Numbers and the public key infrastructure (PKI) certificate associated with those Customer Numbers; and prohibitions on applying for or being added to a USPTO Customer Number until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These administrative steps (publication, notification, dissociation, PKI removal, and Customer Number restrictions) are part of implementing and publicizing the discipline and preventing further unauthorized practice before the USPTO until reinstatement.
